newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-What to watch for from the by-election.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-What to watch for from the by-election.

text.p: Saturday's by-election for the Sydney seat of Lindsay is unlikely to change anything, and for that reason is not too important.
But it will give us some insight into how the government is trading politically.
A massive swing away from the government -- say, eight percentage points -- would show that the government's commanding lead in national opinion polls is soft.
More likely, however, the government may win the by-election, as suggested by the McNair poll in today's Sydney Morning Herald newspaper.

Such an event would confirm the remarkable circumstances that most political observers believe is the case -- that the government, despite its massively deficit-slashing budget and even this week's conflicts of interest turmoil, is riding high.
Think how unlikely a government win should be. Governments tend to lose by-elections and the Liberals should not hold an historically safe Labor seat.
Certainly, governments that have just ripped A$7.2 billion from the budget should be wildly unpopular.
Moreover, voters' traditional by-election psychology should be working very strongly against the government.

Governments tend to suffer in by-elections because voters, knowing that nothing important is riding on the outcome, tend to vote strongly against the government for whatever little sins have recently upset them.
In the average voter's mind, no by-election could have less impact on an administration than this one, where the government holds a massive majority and is more than two years from an election.
So, all things considered, the government should by rights be heading for a punishing defeat on Saturday.
The real news would be that it doesn't get one.
